hiram-revels.excerpt: Mississippi sent America's first Black senator to Washington in 1870. Then the Senate argued for days about whether he was a citizen.
sections: Born free

Hiram Rhodes Revels was born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on 27 September 1827, the son of a Baptist preacher. North Carolina made it illegal to educate Black children, so he learned at a school run by a free Black woman and worked for some years as a barber. In 1844 he went north for an education, to a Quaker seminary in Indiana and a seminary for Black students in Ohio, and from 1855 to 1857 he attended Knox College in Illinois. In 1845 he was ordained in the African Methodist Episcopal Church.

He preached in Indiana, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky and Tennessee. In 1853 he took a church in St Louis, and in 1854 he was imprisoned there for preaching to Black people. He married Phoebe Bass, a free Black woman from Ohio; they had six daughters.
War

In 1861 Revels helped recruit two Black regiments in Maryland, and in 1862 he served as chaplain to a Black regiment in the Vicksburg and Jackson campaigns in Mississippi. In 1863 he founded a school for freed people in St Louis. After the war he served churches in Kansas, Kentucky and Louisiana before settling in Natchez, Mississippi, in 1866. He became an alderman there in 1868, and in 1869, encouraged by the Black politician John Roy Lynch, won a seat in the state senate, one of more than thirty Black members in a legislature of 140.
Chosen by the legislature

At the time, state legislatures chose U.S. senators, not voters. Mississippi had two seats to fill: one once held by Jefferson Davis, who had walked out of the Senate in January 1861 to lead the Confederacy, and one once held by Albert G. Brown. On 20 January 1870 the legislature voted 85 to 15 to send Revels to Washington for Brown's old seat. Davis's went to Adelbert Ames. It is often said that Revels took Jefferson Davis's seat; he did not.
Forty-eight to eight

Senate Democrats, led by Garrett Davis of Kentucky and Willard Saulsbury of Delaware, tried to stop him. Some argued that Mississippi had no lawful government; others that a Black man could not have been a citizen for the nine years the Constitution requires of a senator, since, under the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision, no Black person had been a citizen before the Fourteenth Amendment of 1868. Charles Sumner of Massachusetts answered for Revels, quoting the Declaration of Independence. On 25 February 1870 the Senate voted 48 to 8 to seat him, and Hiram Revels became the first African American to serve in the United States Congress.
A year in the Senate, and after

His term ran only until March 1871. In his first speech, on 16 March 1870, he argued for reinstating the Black legislators who had been expelled in Georgia. He opposed an amendment that would have kept Washington's schools segregated, supported amnesty for former Confederates who showed their loyalty, nominated a Black candidate to West Point, and helped Black mechanics from Baltimore get work at the Navy Yard.

In 1871 he became the first president of Alcorn University in Mississippi, the first land-grant college for Black students in the country. He served as the state's interim secretary of state in 1873, resigned from Alcorn in 1874 rather than be removed by Governor Ames, and returned in 1876. He retired in 1882 to Holly Springs, where he taught theology. Hiram Revels died of a stroke on 16 January 1901, at a church conference in Aberdeen, Mississippi, and is buried in Holly Springs.

ida-b-wells.excerpt: She bit a conductor to keep her seat. Then she sued the railroad, and won, seventy years before Rosa Parks.
sections: The ladies' car

Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, in 1862. As a young teacher she commuted by train between Memphis and the school where she taught in Woodstock, Tennessee. One day in 1883 or 1884, the sources differ, she took her seat in the ladies' car with a first-class ticket, and the conductor ordered her to move to the smoking car. She refused. When he tried to drag her out she fought back; in her autobiography she wrote that she fastened her teeth in the back of his hand. It took the conductor and two other men to remove her from the train, and she got off rather than finish the journey in the other car.
Five hundred dollars, then nothing

Wells sued the Chesapeake, Ohio and Southwestern Railroad, and she won. The circuit court awarded her 500 dollars. Then the Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the decision; the National Park Service dates the reversal to 1885, the Tennessee State Museum to 1887. After that she became more outspoken, writing about racial injustice in the South, and she became a journalist and co-owner of a Memphis newspaper, the Free Speech, which was based in the First Baptist Church on Beale Street.
Memphis, March 1892

In 1892 a white grocer, William Barrett, set out to close a rival, the People's Grocery, a cooperative store run by Black Memphians. One of its owners, Thomas Moss, was a close friend of Wells. In the confrontation that followed shots were fired, and Moss and two other men were jailed. Early on 9 March 1892 they were taken from their cells and killed. Wells investigated and published what she found, and urged Black Memphians to leave the city.

In May 1892, while she was in New York, a mob destroyed the Free Speech office and its presses, and she was warned she would be killed if she returned. She did not. Reports that all three murdered men were her friends appear in only one of our sources; the Tennessee State Museum names Moss as her friend.
The campaign against lynching

From Chicago, Wells spent the rest of her life investigating and exposing lynching. In the 1890s she published Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases and A Red Record, which tabulated lynchings and the excuses given for them. In 1893 she founded a women's club in Chicago and challenged the organisers of the World's Columbian Exposition with a pamphlet on why Black Americans had been left out of it.
Votes for women, and a prize 89 years late

By 1910 Wells had turned to women's suffrage as well. In 1913 she founded the Alpha Suffrage Club, Chicago's first suffrage organisation for Black women; by 1916 it had 200 members and had helped elect Oscar DePriest, the city's first Black alderman. At the great suffrage parade in Washington in 1913, told to march at the back, she waited until the Illinois delegation passed and then stepped out to its front, and a photographer caught the moment.
Ida B. Wells died in 1931. In May 2020 the Pulitzer Prize board awarded her a special citation for her reporting, 89 years after her death.
